claim: Infection with the food-borne liver fluke Opisthorchis viverrini is the principal risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) in the Lower Mekong River Basin countries including Thailand, Lao PDR, Vietnam and Cambodia.
source: Infection with the food-borne liver fluke Opisthorchis viverrini is the principal risk factor (IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, 2012) for cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) in the Lower Mekong River Basin countries including Thailand, Lao PDR, Vietnam and Cambodia.
evidence: Supported by citation to IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, 2012

claim: Deep sequencing of amplicon libraries from genomic DNA of gene-edited parasites revealed Cas9-catalyzed mutations within Ov-GRN-1.
source: Deep sequencing of amplicon libraries from genomic DNA of gene-edited parasites revealed Cas9-catalyzed mutations within Ov-GRN-1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from deep sequencing analysis

claim: Gene editing resulted in rapid depletion of Ov-GRN-1 transcripts and the encoded Ov-GRN-1 protein.
source: Gene editing resulted in rapid depletion of Ov-GRN-1 transcripts and the encoded Ov-GRN-1 protein.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of transcript and protein levels

claim: Gene-edited parasites colonized the biliary tract of hamsters and developed into adult flukes.
source: Gene-edited parasites colonized the biliary tract of hamsters and developed into adult flukes, but the infection resulted in reduced pathology as evidenced by attenuated biliary hyperplasia and fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by in vivo experimental observations in hamster model

claim: Infection with gene-edited parasites resulted in reduced pathology as evidenced by attenuated biliary hyperplasia and fibrosis.
source: Gene-edited parasites colonized the biliary tract of hamsters and developed into adult flukes, but the infection resulted in reduced pathology as evidenced by attenuated biliary hyperplasia and fibrosis.
evidence: Supported by histopathological analysis of infected hamster tissues

claim: This report pioneers programmed gene-editing in parasitic flatworms.
source: Not only does this report pioneer programmed gene-editing in parasitic flatworms, but also the striking, clinically-relevant pathophysiological phenotype confirms the role for Ov-GRN-1 in virulence morbidity during opisthorchiasis.
evidence: Supported by the novelty of the experimental approach and lack of prior reports

claim: The pathophysiological phenotype confirms the role for Ov-GRN-1 in virulence morbidity during opisthorchiasis.
source: Not only does this report pioneer programmed gene-editing in parasitic flatworms, but also the striking, clinically-relevant pathophysiological phenotype confirms the role for Ov-GRN-1 in virulence morbidity during opisthorchiasis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced pathology in gene-edited parasite infections

claim: Approximately 10 million people are infected with O. viverrini in Thailand and Laos.
source: O. viverrini is endemic in Thailand and Laos, where ~10 million people are infected with the parasite (Sripa et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sripa et al., 2011

claim: Liver fluke infection causes hepatobiliary morbidity including cholangitis, choledocholithiasis (gall stones), and periductal fibrosis.
source: In liver fluke endemic regions, this infection causes hepatobiliary morbidity including cholangitis, choledocholithiasis (gall stones), and periductal fibrosis, and is the principal risk factor for bile duct cancer, cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) (Sripa et al., 2011; Sripa et al., 2007; Mairiang et al., 2012; Tyson and El-Serag, 2011; Shin et al., 2010a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: O. viverrini infection is the principal risk factor for bile duct cancer, cholangiocarcinoma (CCA).
source: In liver fluke endemic regions, this infection causes hepatobiliary morbidity including cholangitis, choledocholithiasis (gall stones), and periductal fibrosis, and is the principal risk factor for bile duct cancer, cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) (Sripa et al., 2011; Sripa et al., 2007; Mairiang et al., 2012; Tyson and El-Serag, 2011; Shin et al., 2010a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: There is no stronger link between a human malignancy and a parasitic infection than that between CCA and infection with O. viverrini.
source: Indeed, there is no stronger link between a human malignancy and a parasitic infection than that between CCA and infection with O. viverrini (Pagano et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pagano et al., 2004

claim: Northeastern Thailand suffers the highest incidence of CCA in the world, often exceeding 80 cases per 100,000 population.
source: Northeastern Thailand suffers the highest incidence of CCA in the world, often exceeding 80 cases per 100,000 population and for which up to 20,000 people annually are admitted for surgery.
evidence: Supported by epidemiological data from the region

claim: Up to 20,000 people annually are admitted for surgery for CCA in northeastern Thailand.
source: Northeastern Thailand suffers the highest incidence of CCA in the world, often exceeding 80 cases per 100,000 population and for which up to 20,000 people annually are admitted for surgery.
evidence: Supported by epidemiological data from the region

claim: The prognosis for liver fluke infection-induced cancer remains poor.
source: The prognosis for liver fluke infection-induced cancer remains poor (Sripa et al., 2011; Khuntikeo et al., 2015; Khuntikeo et al., 2016; Luvira et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Opisthorchiasis-induced cholangiocarcinogenesis is likely multi-factorial, including mechanical irritation of the biliary tract during migration and feeding of the liver fluke, secretion by the parasite of inflammatory molecules, and nitrosamines in fermented foods.
source: How and why opisthorchiasis induces cholangiocarcinogenesis is likely multi-factorial, including mechanical irritation of the biliary tract during migration and feeding of the liver fluke, secretion by the parasite of inflammatory molecules, and nitrosamines in fermented foods that are a dietary staple in northeastern provinces of Thailand (Songserm et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation and established knowledge of disease mechanisms

claim: Parasitic helminths produce an assortment of excretory/secretory (ES) products including proteins with diverse roles at the host–parasite interface.
source: To survive in the hostile host environment, parasitic helminths produce an assortment of excretory/secretory (ES) products including proteins with diverse roles at the host–parasite interface.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of helminth biology

claim: Feeding activity of the liver fluke inflicts wounds in the biliary tree, resulting in lesions that undergo protracted cycles of repair and re-injury during chronic infection.
source: Feeding activity of the liver fluke inflicts wounds in the biliary tree, resulting in lesions that undergo protracted cycles of repair and re-injury during chronic infection.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of liver fluke pathology

claim: The liver fluke secretes mediators that accelerate wound resolution in monolayers of cultured cholangiocytes.
source: The liver fluke secretes mediators that accelerate wound resolution in monolayers of cultured cholangiocytes, an outcome that is compromised following silencing of expression of the liver fluke secreted growth factor Ov-GRN-1 using RNA interference (Papatpremsiri et al., 2015; Smout et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies

claim: Wound resolution in cultured cholangiocytes is compromised following silencing of expression of Ov-GRN-1 using RNA interference.
source: The liver fluke secretes mediators that accelerate wound resolution in monolayers of cultured cholangiocytes, an outcome that is compromised following silencing of expression of the liver fluke secreted growth factor Ov-GRN-1 using RNA interference (Papatpremsiri et al., 2015; Smout et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies

claim: Proliferation of biliary epithelial cells induced by Ov-GRN-1 is a pivotal factor in maintenance and progression of a tumorigenic microenvironment in the liver during chronic opisthorchiasis.
source: We hypothesize that proliferation of biliary epithelial cells induced by Ov-GRN-1 is a pivotal factor in maintenance and progression of a tumorigenic microenvironment in the liver during chronic opisthorchiasis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on prior observations

claim: Progress with development of genetic tools for functional genomic studies with platyhelminth parasites has been limited to date.
source: Progress with development of genetic tools for functional genomic studies with platyhelminth parasites has been limited to date (Hoffmann et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior review

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 has revolutionized genome editing in biomedicine, agriculture and biology.
source: The use of clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR) associated with Cas9, an RNA-guided DNA endonuclease, has revolutionized genome editing in biomedicine, agriculture and biology (Hsu et al., 2014; Sander and Joung, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Progress with CRISPR/Cas9 in nematodes Caenorhabditis elegans, Strongyloides stercoralis and Strongyloides ratti has been described.
source: Progress with CRISPR/Cas9 in numerous eukaryotes including the nematodes Caenorhabditis elegans, Strongyloides stercoralis and Strongyloides ratti has been described (Sander and Joung, 2014; Waaijers and Boxem, 2014; Lok et al., 2017; Gang et al., 2017), but this form of gene editing has not been reported for flatworm parasites.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing has not been reported for flatworm parasites prior to this study.
source: Progress with CRISPR/Cas9 in numerous eukaryotes including the nematodes Caenorhabditis elegans, Strongyloides stercoralis and Strongyloides ratti has been described (Sander and Joung, 2014; Waaijers and Boxem, 2014; Lok et al., 2017; Gang et al., 2017), but this form of gene editing has not been reported for flatworm parasites.
evidence: Supported by absence of prior reports in the literature

claim: A reduction in relative fold amplification of 2.7% was detected in gDNA from the Cas9-treated worms.
source: A reduction in relative fold amplification of 2.7% was detected in gDNA from the Cas9-treated worms (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR experimental data shown in figures

claim: Among >2 million reads aligned against the reference sequence, 27,640 sequence reads exhibited non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) mutations.
source: The CRISPResso computational pipeline was used to quantify gene-editing outcomes and efficiency (Canver et al., 2018; Pinello et al., 2016); among >2 million reads aligned against the reference sequence, 27,640 sequence reads exhibited non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) mutations, including 170 reads with insertions (0.6%), 193 reads with deletions (0.7%) and 27,277 reads with substitutions (98.7%).
evidence: Supported by deep sequencing data analysis

claim: Overall, 1.3% of the sequenced reads exhibited NHEJ mutations.
source: Overall, 1.3% of the sequenced reads exhibited NHEJ mutations (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by deep sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: More than 100 forms exhibited mutations that would disrupt the coding sequence of Ov-GRN-1.
source: Regarding the NHEJ-bearing reads,>100 forms exhibited mutations that would disrupt the coding sequencing of Ov-GRN-1.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of NHEJ mutations

claim: Levels of both Ov-GRN-1 mRNA transcripts and Ov-GRN-1 protein fell significantly from days 1 and 2 after transfection, respectively (p≤0.0001).
source: Levels of both Ov-GRN-1 mRNA transcripts as determined by reverse transcription (RT)-qPCR and of Ov-GRN-1 protein, as detected by western blot using anti-Ov-GRN-1 serum, fell significantly from days 1 and 2 after transfection, respectively (p≤0.0001; Figure 1D and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and western blot experimental data shown in figures

claim: Expression levels of actin and Ov-TSP-2 tegument protein were not influenced by the programmed mutation of Ov-GRN-1.
source: Expression levels of two reference genes encoding actin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and the Ov-TSP-2 tegument protein (Figure 1D) were not influenced by the programmed mutation of Ov-GRN-1.
evidence: Supported by control protein expression data shown in figures

claim: ES from WT and mock-transfected adult flukes stimulated cell proliferation and wound closure.
source: ES from WT and mock-transfected adult flukes stimulated cell proliferation and wound closure whereas an equivalent amount of ES products from ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes resulted in significantly reduced cell proliferation over the 6-day course of the assay (p ≤ 0.0001; Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) and significantly reduced in vitro wound closure over 36 hr (p ≤ 0.0001; Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), consistent with the reduction in Ov-GRN-1 protein secreted from the gene-edited liver flukes.
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation and wound healing assay data shown in figures

claim: ES products from ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes resulted in significantly reduced cell proliferation over the 6-day course of the assay (p ≤ 0.0001).
source: ES from WT and mock-transfected adult flukes stimulated cell proliferation and wound closure whereas an equivalent amount of ES products from ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes resulted in significantly reduced cell proliferation over the 6-day course of the assay (p ≤ 0.0001; Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) and significantly reduced in vitro wound closure over 36 hr (p ≤ 0.0001; Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), consistent with the reduction in Ov-GRN-1 protein secreted from the gene-edited liver flukes.
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in figures

claim: ES products from ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes resulted in significantly reduced in vitro wound closure over 36 hr (p ≤ 0.0001).
source: ES from WT and mock-transfected adult flukes stimulated cell proliferation and wound closure whereas an equivalent amount of ES products from ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes resulted in significantly reduced cell proliferation over the 6-day course of the assay (p ≤ 0.0001; Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B) and significantly reduced in vitro wound closure over 36 hr (p ≤ 0.0001; Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D), consistent with the reduction in Ov-GRN-1 protein secreted from the gene-edited liver flukes.
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data shown in figures

claim: Significant differences in Ov-GRN-1 transcript levels were noted between groups of MC (p ≤ 0.01), but the effect was modest, ≤4%, at each time point.
source: Significant differences in Ov-GRN-1 transcript levels were noted between groups of MC (p ≤ 0.01), but the effect was modest, ≤4%, at each time point (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that delivery of the pCas-Ov-GRN-1 by electroporation through the MC cyst wall was ineffective.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in figure supplement

claim: Delivery of the pCas-Ov-GRN-1 by electroporation through the MC cyst wall was ineffective.
source: Significant differences in Ov-GRN-1 transcript levels were noted between groups of MC (p ≤ 0.01), but the effect was modest, ≤4%, at each time point (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that delivery of the pCas-Ov-GRN-1 by electroporation through the MC cyst wall was ineffective.
evidence: Inferred from the modest effect on transcript levels

claim: Marked depletion of Ov-GRN-1 transcripts in NEJ was evident by 24 hr after electroporation (p ≤ 0.0001).
source: Following this manipulation, marked depletion of Ov-GRN-1 transcripts in NEJ was evident by 24 hr later (p ≤ 0.0001) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Similar numbers of WT and ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes were observed in the bile ducts at 14 days post-infection.
source: At necropsy of the hamsters 14 days later, similar numbers of WT and ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes were observed in the bile ducts, and they were similarly motile (not shown).
evidence: Supported by observation during necropsy

claim: Infection with WT flukes induced markedly disordered, hyperplasic growth of the epithelium adjacent to the parasites with ~500% thickening of the biliary epithelium compared to uninfected controls (p ≤ 0.0001).
source: Specifically, infection with WT flukes induced markedly disordered, hyperplasic growth of the epithelium adjacent to the parasites; ~500% thickening of the biliary epithelium compared to uninfected controls as measured in two-dimensional image analysis of H and E-stained thin sections (p ≤ 0.0001).
evidence: Supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: Infection with the ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes provoked significantly less (p ≤ 0.0001) biliary hyperplasia than WT flukes (145% thickening compared to uninfected controls; p ≤ 0.01).
source: By contrast, infection with the ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes provoked significantly less (p ≤ 0.0001) biliary hyperplasia than WT flukes (145% thickening compared to uninfected controls; p ≤ 0.01).
evidence: Supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: The bile ducts from hamsters infected with the ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes generally resembled those of the uninfected control hamsters.
source: Indeed, the bile ducts from hamsters infected with the ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes generally resembled those of the uninfected control hamsters (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by histopathological images shown in Figure 3

claim: At 60 days after infection, significant differences in biliary hyperplasia remained between hamsters infected with WT (216%) and ΔOv-GRN-1 (162%) flukes (p ≤ 0.05).
source: At 60 days after infection, significant differences in biliary hyperplasia remained between hamsters infected with WT (216%) and ΔOv-GRN-1 (162%) flukes (p ≤ 0.05), although this was less marked than during acute infection at day 14 (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by histopathological analysis shown in Figure 3G

claim: Similar numbers of worms were recovered from both control and gene-edited liver fluke-infected hamsters at 60 days post-infection.
source: To evaluate disease during chronic infection with ΔOv-GRN-1 liver flukes and associated chronic biliary morbidity, hamsters were infected with ΔOv-GRN-1 and WT NEJ, and adult flukes were recovered and counted from the livers 60 days post-infection. Similar numbers of worms were recovered from both control and gene-edited liver fluke-infected hamsters (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by worm count data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Thick bands of collagen surrounded the enlarged bile ducts in the vicinity of the flukes in the hamsters infected with WT parasites.
source: Minimal deposits of collagen were seen in the periductal regions of the biliary tract of the uninfected control hamsters. By contrast, thick bands of collagen surrounded the enlarged bile ducts in the vicinity of the flukes in the hamsters infected with WT parasites.
evidence: Supported by Picro-Sirius Red staining shown in Figure 4B

claim: Significantly less collagen (28%) had been deposited in periductal regions of hamsters infected with ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes compared to livers of hamsters infected with WT flukes (p ≤ 0.001).
source: Significantly less collagen (28%) had been deposited in periductal regions of hamsters infected with ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes compared to livers of hamsters infected with WT flukes (p ≤ 0.001) (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of Picro-Sirius Red staining shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: Livers of hamsters infected with WT flukes showed densely packed collagen fibrils that stained for ACTA2 in periductal regions proximal to the parasites.
source: Livers of hamsters infected with WT flukes showed densely packed collagen fibrils that stained for ACTA2 in periductal regions proximal to the parasites.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4D

claim: Livers from hamsters infected with ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes displayed an irregular distribution of less dense collagen fibrils with less ACTA2-specific fluorescence.
source: In contrast, livers from hamsters infected with ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes displayed an irregular distribution of less dense collagen fibrils with less ACTA2-specific fluorescence (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4D and supplement

claim: Median levels of ACTA2 in the livers of ΔOv-GRN-1 fluke-infected hamsters were significantly reduced (94%) compared to those of WT fluke-infected hamsters (p ≤ 0.01).
source: Median levels of ACTA2 (quantified using Alexa-594-anti-ACTA2) in the livers of ΔOv-GRN-1 fluke-infected hamsters were significantly reduced (94%) compared to those of WT fluke-infected hamsters (p ≤ 0.01) (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of ACTA2 fluorescence shown in Figure 4E

claim: Levels of Ov-GRN-1 mRNA in the ΔOv-GRN-1 group flukes were 81% lower, in aggregate, than the control wild-type flukes.
source: This revealed that levels of Ov-GRN-1 mRNA in the ΔOv-GRN-1 group flukes were 81% lower, in aggregate, than the control wild-type flukes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The NGS CRISPResso analysis revealed mutation rates of 1.3, 5.9 and 17.2% in the L, M, and H groups of ΔOv-GRN-1 worms, respectively.
source: The NGS CRISPResso analysis revealed mutation rates of 1.3, 5.9 and 17.2% in the L, M, and H groups of ΔOv-GRN-1 worms, respectively.
evidence: Supported by NGS analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: The tri-primer qPCR analysis indicated mutation levels of 0.7, 3.2 and 4.6% in the L, M, and H groups, respectively.
source: The tri-primer qPCR analysis indicated mutation levels of 0.7, 3.2 and 4.6% in these groups, respectively.
evidence: Supported by qPCR analysis

claim: Both approaches confirmed that the efficiency of programmed gene editing negatively correlated with levels of the Ov-GRN-1 transcripts.
source: Both approaches confirmed that the efficiency of programmed gene editing negatively correlated with levels of the Ov-GRN-1 transcripts (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of mutation rates and transcript levels shown in Figure 5

claim: The combined mutation frequency among all three groups by the two approaches was 8.1% and 2.7%.
source: The combined mutation frequency among all three groups by the two approaches was 8.1% and 2.7%, with the 2.7% rate estimated by tri-primer qPCR indicating the same level as the mutation rate of 2.7% observed during culture of adult stage ΔOv-GRN-1 flukes for 7 to 21 days in vitro (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by combined analysis of NGS and qPCR data

claim: Mutations were retained in the parasite for at least 60 days during active infection of the mammalian host.
source: Lastly, these findings also demonstrated the longevity of the programmed mutation at Ov-GRN-1; mutations were retained in the parasite for at least 60 days during active infection of the mammalian host.
evidence: Supported by detection of mutations in flukes recovered 60 days post-infection

claim: The somatic mutation rate in the adult developmental stage was generally <5% of the genomes recovered from these multicellular parasites.
source: Although the findings demonstrated programmed gene editing of the Ov-GRN-1 locus, the somatic mutation rate in the adult developmental stage was generally <5% of the genomes recovered from these multicellular parasites.
evidence: Supported by mutation rate analysis from genomic DNA

claim: Ov-GRN-1 exhibits generalized expression throughout tissues of the adult liver fluke, with predominant expression immunolocalized to the tegumental surface, tegumental cytons and gut.
source: Although it exhibits generalized expression throughout tissues of the adult liver fluke, predominant expression of Ov-GRN-1 has been immunolocalized to the tegumental surface, tegumental cytons and gut (Smout et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior immunolocalization study

claim: The activity in vitro of liver fluke granulin in cell proliferation, wound repair and angiogenesis has been established.
source: The activity in vitro of liver fluke granulin in cell proliferation, wound repair and angiogenesis has been established (Papatpremsiri et al., 2015; Smout et al., 2015; Smout et al., 2009), which has prompted the development of therapeutic peptides based on the Ov-GRN-1 scaffold for treatment of non-healing wounds (Bansal et al., 2017; Dastpeyman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior experimental studies

claim: Therapeutic peptides based on the Ov-GRN-1 scaffold have been developed for treatment of non-healing wounds.
source: The activity in vitro of liver fluke granulin in cell proliferation, wound repair and angiogenesis has been established (Papatpremsiri et al., 2015; Smout et al., 2015; Smout et al., 2009), which has prompted the development of therapeutic peptides based on the Ov-GRN-1 scaffold for treatment of non-healing wounds (Bansal et al., 2017; Dastpeyman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies on therapeutic peptide development

claim: Programmed gene editing confirmed that secreted parasite granulin induces hyperplasia of the biliary epithelium and fibrosis during chronic infection.
source: Programmed gene editing confirmed that secreted parasite granulin induces hyperplasia of the biliary epithelium and fibrosis during chronic infection, and that liver fluke granulin directly contributes to morbidity of the hepatobiliary tract during both acute and chronic opisthorchiasis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from gene-edited parasite infections

claim: Liver fluke granulin directly contributes to morbidity of the hepatobiliary tract during both acute and chronic opisthorchiasis.
source: Programmed gene editing confirmed that secreted parasite granulin induces hyperplasia of the biliary epithelium and fibrosis during chronic infection, and that liver fluke granulin directly contributes to morbidity of the hepatobiliary tract during both acute and chronic opisthorchiasis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from gene-edited parasite infections

claim: The impact of Ov-GRN-1 might emulate the action of interleukin IL−33, an epithelial mitogen for cholangiocytes, in the development of CCA.
source: The impact of Ov-GRN-1 might emulate the action of interleukin IL−33, an epithelial mitogen for cholangiocytes, in the development of CCA.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison proposed by the authors

claim: IL-33 primes type two innate lymphoid cells to induce proliferation of neighboring cholangiocytes by the release of IL-13.
source: IL-33 primes type two innate lymphoid cells to induce proliferation of neighboring cholangiocytes by the release of IL-13 (Brindley and Loukas, 2017; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The bacterial Type II Cas9 system is active in O. viverrini.
source: Accordingly, the findings confirmed that the bacterial Type II Cas9 system is active in O. viverrini, and we suggest that Cas9-mediated programmed gene editing and repair by homology directed repair and NHEJ will be active in other genes of the liver fluke, and in other trematodes and parasitic platyhelminths generally.
evidence: Supported by experimental demonstration of Cas9 activity

claim: Cas9-mediated programmed gene editing and repair by homology directed repair and NHEJ will be active in other genes of the liver fluke, and in other trematodes and parasitic platyhelminths generally.
source: Accordingly, the findings confirmed that the bacterial Type II Cas9 system is active in O. viverrini, and we suggest that Cas9-mediated programmed gene editing and repair by homology directed repair and NHEJ will be active in other genes of the liver fluke, and in other trematodes and parasitic platyhelminths generally.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the successful demonstration in O. viverrini

claim: The chromosomal break took place as programmed and was repaired subsequently by NHEJ following Cas9-catalyzed mutation.
source: Scrutiny of the nucleotide sequence reads indicated that the chromosomal break took place as programmed and was repaired subsequently by NHEJ following Cas9-catalyzed mutation (Albadri et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis of mutations

claim: Gene knockout of the target Ov-GRN-1 locus in nuclei of cells in the tegument and gut may have occurred more frequently than in cells deeper within the fluke.
source: Given that the flukes were transfected in vitro with the gene editing plasmid by square wave electroporation, gene knockout of the target Ov-GRN-1 locus in nuclei of cells in the tegument and gut may have occurred more frequently than in cells deeper within the fluke.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern of gene editing

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-based gene editing and the hamster model of human opisthorchiasis provide a facile, functional genomics system to interrogate the host-parasite relationship and pathophysiology.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-based gene editing and the hamster model of human opisthorchiasis utilized here (Sripa et al., 2007), including genetic manipulation of the larval infective stage of the parasite, provide a facile, functional genomics system to interrogate this host-parasite relationship and pathophysiology (Hoffmann et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by the successful application of the approach in this study

claim: Metacercariae of O. viverrini were isolated from naturally infected cyprinid fish by pepsin digestion.
source: Metacercariae (MC) of O. viverrini were isolated from the naturally infected cyprinid fish by pepsin digestion as described (Pinlaor et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to established protocol

claim: The Animal Ethics Committee of Khon Kaen University approved the study, approval number ACUC-KKU-61/60.
source: The Animal Ethics Committee of Khon Kaen University approved the study, approval number ACUC-KKU-61/60, which adhered to standard guidelines of the National Research Council of Thailand for the Ethics of Animal Experimentation.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical approval
